deterrent

/dih-TUR-uhnt/ - the stress falls on TUR · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Deterrent means something that discourages an action by making its consequences feared; it works in advance, in the mind of whoever is weighing the act.

The dye packs cost the bank almost nothing, but their value as a deterrent has been priceless: three years now without a single robbery attempt.

Example

When the city hung bright-orange speed cameras over Millbrook Road, the council braced for an avalanche of fines. It never came — barely two hundred tickets all year, against nine thousand projected. Drivers spotted the cameras three blocks out and slowed; the deterrent was doing its work in windshields and rearview mirrors, and the punishments were hardly ever needed.

That gap between tickets projected and tickets written is the signature of a deterrent: it discourages the act in advance, by making the consequence feared, and it succeeds exactly to the degree that it never has to fire. Had the city hidden the cameras and mailed nine thousand fines, it would have had punishment. Visible and feared, it had prevention.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disincentive: A disincentive quietly tilts the arithmetic of a choice — a fee, a tax, a hassle that makes the act less rewarding. A deterrent works on the nerves instead: it threatens, and fear of the consequence does the discouraging even if the penalty is never once applied.

curb: A curb is a check on something already underway — spending curbs rein in a budget that is moving. A deterrent gets there earlier: it discourages the act before it starts, in the mind of whoever is weighing it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

incentive: a promised reward that pulls people toward an act

enticement: a temptation dangled to draw someone in

Where it sits · how forcefully the act is discouraged

disincentive → deterrent → prohibition

disincentive vs. deterrent: A disincentive is milder than a deterrent: a fee or a hassle that quietly tilts the arithmetic of a choice, where a deterrent plants real fear of a consequence.

prohibition vs. deterrent: Prohibition goes further than a deterrent: a deterrent loads the choice with fear but leaves it open, while a prohibition removes the choice entirely and backs the ban with law.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-: away, off (Latin)

Root — terr: to frighten (Latin terrēre)

Suffix — -ent: the thing or agent that does it

Put it together: De- (away) + terrēre (to frighten) + -ent (the agent that does it) assembles 'the thing that frightens you off' — a complete job description. A deterrent never has to act; it only has to be believed in. The root keeps its fright out in the open elsewhere in English: terror, terrify, and terrible all carry it.

Use the root in a new word: terrific: A terrific crash of falling scaffolding emptied the square in seconds.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / policy, law, and security

Deterrent belongs to arguments about crime, war, and rule-breaking: the posted fine, the visible camera, the arsenal maintained so that it never has to be used. Keep it apart from an obstacle, which physically blocks, and a punishment, which arrives after the act — a deterrent does its work beforehand, in the imagination. And spell with care: detergent only fights stains.
